turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The car park was a proper circus, I did three loops and a bloke in a ute just sat there indicating and not moving.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're right, no stress. Have a seat.
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): I grabbed a fishing magazine out there and I don't even fish, I just hate staring at the wall. Told my neighbour this morning the weather can't make up its mind.

[SEG0004] person_3 (NURSE): I'll put the obs in before you start. Temp is thirty-seven point four, pulse eighty-eight, blood pressure one twenty-two over seventy-six, sats ninety-nine percent on room air.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ta, those are comfortable. What are we actually here for today?

[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay I over-explain, sorry. Long weekend up the coast with mates, cheap motel, and on the Saturday we stopped at those roadside stalls with the eskies. I had prawn skewers, satay chicken and a mango cup, went back for a second skewer, chilli and all, felt fine at the time.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): And then what changed?
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): My eyes have gone yellow, my wee is really dark, and I'm exhausted.
[SEG0009] person_2 (DOCTOR): When did you first notice the eyes?
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, I can't pin the day. I thought the motel light was weird, then Dave said I looked off, and Saturday versus Sunday I could not tell you.
[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Are we talking days, or weeks?
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Days. Maybe four or five days for the eyes. I recount on my fingers and I get a different answer every time.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): What about the tiredness?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): A week-ish. I fell asleep on the couch at four in the arvo, which I never do, I'm usually up at six walking the dog, and this morning the kettle felt heavy.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): And the urine, same sort of window?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): Dark like tea. I skulled two bottles of water in case I was just dry from the drive, and it stayed dark. That's the bit that really spooked me.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any fever, or shakes?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): No. No fever. The little thermometer at home sat around thirty-six something, I didn't keep the decimal, but it wasn't up.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Vomiting? Diarrhoea?

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting. One loose stool the day after the stalls, just the once, then it settled. The stools are pale now though, clay coloured, which is new, I'm normally clockwork.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any pain in the belly?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. If I go looking for it there's a niggle and then it's gone, so I wouldn't swear to it.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Itching anywhere?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No itch. I checked in the full-length mirror this morning, top to toe, nothing. No rash either, skin looks like my usual skin.
[SEG0025] person_3 (NURSE): Not short of breath? You came up those stairs pretty quick.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No, not short of breath. That puff was me being late, not my chest.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me think out loud. Yellow whites, tea-coloured wee, pale stool, that's bilirubin, so liver or bile. Roadside seafood is a classic setup for hepatitis A. I'm not calling it, though.

[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): Two of the others got crook off the same prawns. Dave was vomiting for two days, and his sister, she's not my sister, had the runs. He texted this morning still off his food.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shared food, shared illness, that fits something food-borne. Doesn't name it. Do you drink alcohol?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I don't drink. Never have, really. Dad was a big drinker and I never started. One sip of champagne at a wedding, hated it, end of experiment.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Helpful, alcohol can stir up the liver and I can set that aside. Any medicines, chemist stuff included?

[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Panadol, uh paracetemol. Five hundred milligram tablets. I take two, so a thousand milligrams, twice a day, for this headache-y worn out feeling, for about four days. Stayed under the eight-tablet max, I only have four tablets in a day.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Anything else? A script, a vitamin, a herb?

[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): A green and white capsule from the health shop, supposed to be for liver support. Smells like fish. I took it for a few days on the trip and then I stopped because of the burping. Name's gone, the label peeled off on the fridge.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stopped, and you can't name it. Did it give you a rash or swelling, or just burps?
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): Just burping. No rash, no swelling. I wouldn't call that an allergy. Panadol's always been fine.
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines or food, full stop?
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): No, nothing. Never. Nuts are fine, and the dentist has used penicillin, no drama.
[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Past hepatitis, gallstones, any liver disease? Any operations?
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): No, never. No operations. Appendix is still in, tonsils too. I mostly only see a GP for the flu jab, had that at the chemist back in April.
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): In the family, hepatitis or liver problems?
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. Mum's got high blood pressure and she's on a water tablet, but that's her tablet not mine. I live alone, just me and Biscuit, he's a bitser.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Looking at you now, the whites are definitely yellow. Liver edge under the right ribs is a little tender, not hard. Abdomen is soft, no swelling. Skin isn't particularly yellow in this light.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, tender right there. I didn't notice it at home. I also fell down a midnight internet hole about liver failure, dramatic headlines, completely unhelpful.

[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): I wouldn't call this liver failure. It fits an acute hepatitis better. Possibly hepatitis A from that food, and I can't rule out another hepatitis or a bit of bile blockage. Provisional only, the bloods have to speak.
[SEG0046] person_1 (PATIENT): I work in accounts at the council, desk all day, not much exercise, if you need that. Boss gave me the arvo off so I can stay for blood tests.
[SEG0047] person_2 (DOCTOR): I'll order liver blood tests, the full liver panel, and hepatitis serology, A, B and C. Those are happening, not a maybe.
[SEG0048] person_3 (NURSE): I'll print the path form. Downstairs can usually take you today if you go straight there.
[SEG0049] person_2 (DOCTOR): If the bilirubin comes back very high, or it looks like a blockage pattern, we might do an ultrasound then. Not booking that today.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): Do I keep the panadol, the thousand milligrams twice a day? The headache is still there a bit, behind the eyes, not terrible.

[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hold the paracetamol. It can muddy the liver tests. Cool cloth if the head aches, plenty of water, rest, no alcohol, and skip the roadside seafood until this settles. If you turn drowsy or confused, or you start vomiting and can't keep water down, go to emergency, don't wait.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): Cloth, water, rest, emergency if I'm drowsy or spewing. When do I see you?
[SEG0053] person_2 (DOCTOR): Review in one week. We'll look at the results either way. Reception can book it on the way out.
[SEG0054] person_3 (NURSE): I'll walk you down and make sure the form and that appointment both get done.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

omissions.text: Current/recent paracetamol use was specifically quantified as 500 mg tablets, taking 2 tablets (1000 mg) twice daily, with total intake 4 tablets/day and explicitly staying under the maximum 8 tablets/day.
Dark urine was described as 'dark like tea' and persisted despite drinking two bottles of water.
Pale stools were described as clay-coloured and new for the patient.
Abdominal pain history is incompletely captured: patient reported at most an intermittent mild 'niggle' that comes and goes and was not sure it counted as pain.
Negative finding missing: no diarrhoea currently; only one loose stool the day after the food exposure, then it settled.
Negative finding missing: with the supplement, there was no rash or swelling; only burping, and the patient did not consider this an allergy.
Allergy history detail missing: patient denied any medicine or food allergies, specifically saying nuts are fine and penicillin previously caused no problem.
Physical examination detail missing: abdomen was soft.
Investigation plan detail missing: hepatitis serology was specified to include hepatitis A, B and C.
